b.answer:
Worked example: the OpenAI Agents SDK quick-start, changed to quote Harvest Lane prices. Copy install names and imports from the current quick-start; they change between versions.

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install openai-agents
export OPENAI_API_KEY="…"     # spend limit set in the dashboard first
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

@function_tool
def get_price(product: str) -> dict:
    """Today's Harvest Lane price for ONE product, e.g. tatashe."""
    prices = {"tomato": 12500, "tatashe": 9000, "onion": 4000}
    for k, v in prices.items():
        if k in product.lower():
            return {"found": True, "price": v}
    return {"found": False}

agent = Agent(name="Harvest Lane helper",
              instructions="Answer briefly. Use get_price before giving any price.",
              tools=[get_price])

result = Runner.run_sync(agent, "How much is tatashe today?")
print(result.final_output)

My change: added the get_price tool and new instructions to the quick-start's example.

Where the loop hides:

  • @function_tool builds the tool definition (name, description from the docstring, input schema from the type hints): my TOOLS list.
  • Runner.run_sync is my ask(): it calls the model, runs tools on a tool request, sends results back and repeats.
  • Its max_turns setting is my max_turns (check the default in the docs).
  • The SDK's tracing shows each call, like my print("→ …") lines.
mistakes: Copying install names or imports from an old blog post instead of the current quick-start.
Hard-coding the API key in the script to get it running quickly.
No spend limit set before running.
Running the example unchanged, or not being able to map the framework's parts to the hand-written loop.
b.pass: A screenshot of the quick-start running with one visible change (new instructions or a new tool), and a short note pointing to the framework's equivalents of the tool definitions, the loop, and the turn limit.
b.redo: Send it back if nothing was changed, the key appears in code or a screenshot, or the note can't say where the loop happens.

s.answer:
Worked example: agent.py with a third tool and a live price lookup through n8n.

import os, requests
from datetime import date as Date

AREAS = {"bodija", "mokola", "ring road", "akobo", "jericho"}
HOLIDAYS = {"2026-10-01", "2026-12-25"}
PRICE_URL = os.environ["HL_PRICE_WEBHOOK"]   # n8n production webhook URL

def check_delivery_date(date: str, area: str) -> dict:
    d = Date.fromisoformat(date)              # bad format raises: becomes is_error
    a = area.lower().strip()
    if a not in AREAS:       return {"delivers": False, "reason": "area not covered"}
    if d.weekday() == 6:     return {"delivers": False, "reason": "no Sunday delivery"}
    if date in HOLIDAYS:     return {"delivers": False, "reason": "public holiday"}
    return {"delivers": True, "reason": "ok"}

def get_price(product: str) -> dict:
    r = requests.post(PRICE_URL, json={"product": product}, timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()

Add check_delivery_date to TOOLS (inputs date as YYYY-MM-DD and area, both required) and to RUN, and put today's date in SYSTEM.

# test_agent.py
from agent import ask, check_delivery_date

def test_normal():
    assert check_delivery_date("2026-10-05", "Akobo")["delivers"] is True

def test_unknown_input():
    assert check_delivery_date("2026-10-05", "Lekki")["reason"] == "area not covered"

def test_tool_failure():
    # run with n8n stopped, or HL_PRICE_WEBHOOK pointing at a dead URL
    reply = ask("How much is tatashe?")
    assert "Tolu" in reply or "sorry" in reply.lower()

pytest: 3 passed. With n8n stopped, the trace shows get_price returning a tool error, and the agent says: "Sorry, I can't check prices right now. Tolu will follow up shortly." No traceback.
mistakes: No timeout on requests.post, so a dead n8n hangs the agent instead of failing.
Catching the error inside the tool and returning a made-up price instead of letting it reach the model as is_error.
Putting the webhook URL or a key in the code instead of the environment.
Tests that only cover the happy path, or that are run once by hand and not written down.
Using the n8n test URL, which only works while the editor is listening.
s.pass: agent.py has check_delivery_date and one tool calling n8n or a sheet with a timeout; three written tests (normal, unknown input, tool failure) pass; and a run with n8n switched off shows a polite reply, not a traceback.
s.redo: Send it back if any test is missing or failing, there's no timeout, secrets or URLs are hard-coded, or switching off n8n still crashes the program.

g.answer:
Worked example: Harvest Lane's 4.4 policy agent, ported from n8n to Python with the hand-written loop. Same tools (search_policies via an n8n webhook that runs the Supabase search, and get_price), same system message, same model, same 10 questions.

n8n agentPython agent
Correct (of 10)99
Average reply time7.1 s5.8 s
Average tokens per question6,4005,900
Time to build1.5 h4 h
Time to change one rule and re-test5 min15 min (edit, commit, test, redeploy)
Who else can change itTolu, in the editorA developer

Both failed the same question (an unclear slang message), so the gap is the instructions, not the platform. Python was a little faster and cheaper because it sent fewer tokens per call.

Recommendation: For most small-business clients I'd build in n8n: it's quicker to build, the owner can see and change it, and it already handles triggers, retries and approvals. I'd use code when the agent must live inside the client's own app or backend, when their developers will maintain it, or when volume is high enough that small speed and token savings add up. Often the best answer is both: a code agent in the app whose tools call tested n8n workflows.

Submit: both builds (workflow export with credentials removed, and the repository without .env), the shared test set, the results table and the paragraph.
mistakes: Changing the instructions, tools or model between versions, so the comparison isn't fair.
Comparing accuracy only, without speed, cost or build-and-change time.
Leaving keys in the exported workflow or committing .env.
A recommendation based on preference ("code is more professional") rather than the numbers collected.
g.pass: Two versions with the same tools and instructions, both passing the same 10-question test set, a table comparing accuracy, speed, cost and build/change time, and a recommendation that cites those numbers.
g.redo: Send it back if the versions differ in tools or instructions, either fails the shared tests, numbers are missing, or secrets are included in the submission.
